extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers interested in foundations of mathematics (undergraduate/early graduate level); readers of philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: An introductory/expository lecture-style overview of paradoxes that arise from the naive notion of sets and the principal responses (theory of types, axiomatic ZF/ZFC, issues around the Axiom of Choice and Banach–Tarski). Emphasizes conceptual explanation with informal statements of axioms and illustrative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naive notion of a set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set, as it is naively understood, is just a collection of anything you like (e.g., sets of numbers, all stars in the universe, all mice on earth, collections can be nested).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expansive conception is adequate for practical uses but harbors foundational paradoxes (notably Russell's paradox). The text uses examples (numbers, stars, mice, nested sets) to show how naive comprehension leads to trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the set of all sets that are not members of themselves (the Russell set); either it is a member of itself or not, and each choice leads to contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shown compactly and via reductio arguments. Connected to liar paradox and diagonalization. Demonstrates that the naive comprehension principle must be abandoned or restricted: 'Either the Russell set is a member of the Russell set or it is not' leads to contradiction; the conjunction of two reductio conclusions yields an explicit contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: As a liar paradox / self-reference connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's paradox depends essentially on self-reference, analogous to the liar sentence 'This sentence is false.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallel presentations show how self-application produces oscillating truth-values or membership statuses. Use this parallel to motivate why naive comprehension is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: As a diagonalization / Cantor connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Russell's paradox is related to diagonalization arguments (as in Cantor's theorem) insofar as it constructs an entity that eludes a purported mapping/classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains indicator-function view: listing all sets 'in' or 'out' of the Russell set produces a mapping that the Russell set eludes. Use diagonalization intuition to see why the Russell set cannot be well-defined under naive assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vicious-Circle Principle (Russell's proposed restriction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever involves all of a collection must not be one of the collection; conversely, if a collection's total would make some members definable only in terms of that total then the collection has no total.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to preclude all self-referential, liar-like paradoxes. But it is very strong and overreaching: it can render legitimate definitions nonsense (e.g., 'the oldest person in the village' or 'the largest element of a set' can be unjustly disallowed). The text criticizes its vagueness (difference between 'definable' and 'only definable').

rubrics_metrics.name: Russell's Theory of Types
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive solution that places sets/predicates in a hierarchy of types (type 0 = individuals, type 1 = properties of individuals, type 2 = properties of properties, ...), forbidding predicates applying to objects of the same type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets arise as extensions of predicates and inherit the type of the predicate that defines them; applying a predicate to itself is meaningless in the system, so the Russell set cannot be formed. The theory prevents 'set is member of itself' questions by making them ill-typed (nonsense), but it yields multiple notions of 'set' (types) and is complex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic approach / Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) formulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than asking what a set 'really is', axiomatic set theory gives a formal language and a collection of axioms (ZF, or ZFC with Choice) that specify truths about sets sufficient to do mathematics without paradox.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operate within a formal language (strings of symbols). The axioms limit permitted sentences (e.g., ¬∀A (A ∈ U) for a universal set). The axiomatic approach is compared to chess rules: the substance comes from rules that allow some configurations and forbid others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Extensionality
rubrics_metrics.description: If two sets A and B have the same elements, then they are equal. (Formal: ∀A ∀B [∀x (x ∈ A ⇔ x ∈ B) ⇒ A = B])
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decodes to: two sets are the same iff they have the same members. Examples: {a,b}, {b,a}, {a,b,a,a} are the same set. This is an early and key axiom characterizing sets by their members alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null set (empty set) axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a set, denoted ∅, which has no elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The empty set provides a set-theoretic embodiment of zero and allows constructions of natural numbers independently of physical objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pair axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any sets A and B, there exists a set {A, B} containing A and B as its only elements (and in particular {A} exists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to build finite sets and as a building block in constructions of numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: For every set A there exists its power set P(A), whose elements are all subsets of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to Cantor's theorem (P(A) has strictly greater cardinality than A) and is central to discussions of sizes of infinite sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: For every set A, there exists ⋃A, the union of A, whose elements are all the elements of the elements of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows flattening one level of set nesting and is a standard set-construction axiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an infinite set Z that contains ∅ and is closed under the successor operation (if A ∈ Z then ⋃{A,{A}} ∈ Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees the existence of an inductive set from which the natural numbers can be constructed within set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation schema (axiom of separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every set A and every given property φ (a first-order formula), there is a set containing exactly the elements of A that satisfy φ. (Separation is an axiom schema—one axiom for each formula φ.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crucial for escaping Russell's paradox: comprehension is restricted to subsets of an existing set, so the Russell property cannot produce a problematic set unless it were a subset of some A; reductio shows no such A exists, hence no Russell set is formed. The text emphasizes that Separation (not full unrestricted comprehension) resolves the paradox within ZF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement schema
rubrics_metrics.description: For every definable function with domain a set A, there is a set whose elements are all the values of the function. (Replacement is an axiom schema.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacement is a stronger schema implying many existence results; Replacement implies Separation in ZF and is used for building images of sets under definable operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundation axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Every non-empty set A contains an ∈-minimal element (an element of A that has no element in common with A), i.e., no infinite descending ∈-chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precludes pathological membership cycles and supports the iterative conception of sets; part of the standard ZF axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Choice (AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every set A of pairwise-disjoint non-empty sets, there exists a set that contains exactly one element from each set in A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinctive because it asserts existence without providing a method of selecting elements. AC is equivalent to the Well-Ordering Theorem (every set can be well-ordered). It enables constructions that are non-constructive and controversial (e.g., existence of non-measurable sets).

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-ordering equivalence to AC
rubrics_metrics.description: The axiom of choice is logically equivalent to the assertion that every set can be well-ordered (i.e., has a linear ordering in which every non-empty subset has a least element).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use: if every set is well-ordered, pick the least element as the choice; conversely, AC gives a method to define least elements recursively. The text emphasizes the unintuitive nature of a universal well-ordering for arbitrary sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-measurable sets arising from AC
rubrics_metrics.description: All known examples of non-measurable sets (sets to which no additive measure can be assigned) are constructed using the axiom of choice; such sets are non-constructible in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-measurable sets illustrate problems with AC: one cannot explicitly exhibit the members of such sets or give a prescription for their construction. This non-constructibility fuels philosophical resistance to AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banach–Tarski paradox (and its reliance on AC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A solid ball in Euclidean space can be decomposed into finitely many (five) pieces and reassembled by isometries to yield two balls of the same size as the original; four pieces are continuum-sized and one is countable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key point: decomposition uses non-measurable sets and the axiom of choice; the paradox shows doubling of volume under volume-preserving isometries only because the pieces are non-measurable. Banach–Tarski provides an indirect demonstration of the existence of non-measurable sets and a philosophical dilemma about accepting AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative conception vs. type theory; axiomatization trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Type theory resolves paradoxes by hierarchy of types; an iterative notion of sets can remove type distinctions; axiomatic ZF avoids typed multiplicity by giving axioms instead of a metaphysical account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade-offs: type theory yields many kinds of 'sets' by type and is complex; iterative conception or axiomatic approach strive to produce a single notion of set appropriate for mathematics. The text notes costs of each approach and invites comparison of 'good and bad' aspects.
